newsitem.title: CHINA: China jails Tibetan monk in reincarnation row.
newsitem.headline: China jails Tibetan monk in reincarnation row.

text.p: A Chinese court has jailed a Tibetan monk for six years for colluding with the Dalai Lama in the search for the reincarnation of the region's second holiest monk, a court official said on Wednesday.

China's official Xinhua news agency said a court in Xigaze prefecture had convicted Qazha Qamba Chilai, a former Tibetan official, of trying to split the country and leaking state secrets after a trial behind closed doors. It did not elaborate.

A court official reached by telephone in Xigaze said Qazha Qamba Chilai was a monk who colluded with Tibet's exiled spiritual leader the Dalai Lama in a search for the reincarnation of the 10th Panchen Lama, who died in 1989.
Qazha Qamba Chilai, whose Tibetan name is Chadrel Rinpoche, was head of the committee that ran the Tashilunpo lamasery -- the Panchen Lama's seat -- and the search team.
The Dalai Lama announced in May, 1995, his recognition of a six-year-old Tibetan boy, Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, as the new Panchen Lama.
"During (selection of) the soul boy, he (Chadrel Rinpoche) colluded with the Dalai Lama," the court official said.
The Dalai Lama's move enraged atheist China which named another six-year-old Tibetan, Gyaincain Norbu, instead.
Many Tibetans see the Beijing-anointed boy as a false pretender. The whereabouts of Gedhun Choekyi Nyima are not known.

Chadrel Rinpoche was dismissed in mid-1995 as vice-chairman of Tibet's Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, an advisory group to the local parliament. He has been in state custody ever since.

Co-defendants, Qamba Qung, a former government official, and Samzhub, a businessman, were sentenced to four and two years in prison respectively, Xinhua said. Both men are Tibetans but their relationship to Chadrel Rinpoche was not known.
The defendants "colluded with separatist forces abroad", Xinhua quoted the verdict as saying.
"They have seriously jeopardised the national unification and unity of ethnic groups, damaged the stability and development of Tibet and have committed the crime of splitting the country," it said.
Xinhua said all three defendants confessed.
The sentences were handed down on April 21, the agency said without giving a reason for the delay in reporting them.
The sentences went into effect on May 5 after the three defendants "indicated acceptance of the rulings and would not appeal", it said.
China has come under fire from rights groups and Western governments for its heavy-handed treatment of those seeking independence for Tibet.
Beijing dismisses such criticism as interference in its internal affairs and has slammed the West for using Tibet as a tool to split China.
Chinese troops marched into Tibet in 1951 and suppressed a rebellion in the remote and mountainous region in 1959 that forced the Dalai Lama and thousands of followers to flee into exile in India.
The Dalai Lama won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his non-violent campaign for more autonomy for his homeland.
Tibet has been rocked in recent years by sporadic, sometimes violent, anti-Chinese unrest, with monks and nuns often at the forefront of demonstrations for independence.

Authorities tightened security and launched a manhunt across the deeply religious region, which borders India, Nepal, Bhutan and Burma, after a bomb exploded on Christmas Day outside government offices in Tibet's capital, Lhasa.
